question: Is there a meaningful continuity from VOC cinnamon labour to nineteenth-century British plantation labour?
mechanism: Both regimes orient labour and territory toward export commodities under external commercial power, but the labour institutions and production geographies differ sharply. VOC cinnamon relied on caste/service corvée among local populations and late-eighteenth-century gardens concentrated in the coastal low country; British coffee and tea increasingly mobilised wage/contract migration from South India in newly opened central highland estates after 1815. The continuity is therefore in export orientation, colonial administrative capacity and value extraction, not in a single unchanged labour institution or direct reuse of the same plantation lands.
transmission_channel: export commodity demand -> colonial administrative/port capacity and labour mobilisation -> territorial opening after 1815 -> reorganised plantation capitalism
time_lag: 18th-century VOC cinnamon regime to late-1830s and later British estate recruitment
scale: Z1 labour obligation and coastal gardens to Z3 island export economy and highland plantation system
bounded_by: Do not describe Salagama/chalia corvée as the direct institutional ancestor of Indian Tamil estate labour, and do not imply direct land continuity from VOC cinnamon gardens to British coffee/tea estates. RUN44 supports a spatial rupture: coastal cinnamon versus predominantly Kandyan-highland coffee/tea. The continuity is institutional/macro-economic and comparative, not genealogical or cadastral.
